P1.evidence: No setter notes or application referenced anywhere in the call — the only notes in play were the rep's own, and the prospect twice asked to be sent them. The frame covered where he wants to go and the disqualification promise but not where he is, what is in the way or what he needs: 'go over what you're actually trying to achieve, see if we can help you with that... if I feel like it's not the best fit, I'll point you in the right direction, okay?'. Agreement taken ('Sure, no problem') and the open question asked cleanly.

P2.evidence: Injuries were handled properly and with duration — 'How long have you had that chronic back pain for?', 'Where do you think that that came from?', then a second sweep for anything else which produced whole-body stiffness scored 10/10. Training week established at once or twice versus four or five before. Diet asked, although the rep noted he had forgotten to. Sleep picked up intelligently off the painkillers: 'So your sleep also isn't the best from what I'm hearing, if you need to take Advil in the night'. The failure is work: it was never asked, and the fact that the prospect is a construction business owner with his own sales team only emerged at 01:07, after the price and during the objection. Health conditions and hereditary history were never asked; energy was raised leadingly.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals work in the batch. 'What is it mainly about your current physique that you just don't like?' opened it, 'Why is that important for you to actually go to that point now? So many people, when they pass forty, like, I don't care anymore' bridged out of the physical and produced the kids, and 'how do you think that you would show up with your kids when that's the case?' followed by 'And your grandkids in the future?' drove it through to legacy. The reflect-back was delivered explicitly: 'it sounds like the bigger picture, of course you want to get ripped, you want to have like a six pack... but it sounds like more so you just also want to be there with your kids.'

P4.evidence: Ran nearly complete. 'Have you like always done it alone? Have you done it with a trainer?' produced the full history; 'when you work with those PTs, are they not able to just keep you accountable and keep you to the things that you should be doing instead of you just sort of flaking on them?' produced the travel pattern; 'Why do you think that you quit?' produced boredom and forgetting the reason; and 'what do you need from us to make sure that we're going to be different for you than everything that you've tried so far?' let him name it himself. Only the scripted 'the information isn't the problem' line never ran.

P5.evidence: 'Where do you think that you will be at it in like 10 years from now?' produced the darkest answer in the batch — 'very stiff, sluggish, crappy, just not loving yourself... shame of yourself... why are you even living'. The settle question ran close to verbatim: 'I am just curious, would you be willing to settle for that?', answered 'No, I know. You're right. I really need to make a change and drastic change and hold on to it.' 'Why not?' was never asked. The line in the sand appeared only as a description of starting rather than as a question, though 'Are you willing to make that commitment?' partly covers it.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran twice and well, including 'do you believe in yourself that you can actually get to the goals without giving up once?' answered 'Yes. I believe, I believe.' But at the gate the answers turned soft — 'I think so. Yeah, maybe', 'It's not so certain', and then 'Yeah, I'm on the fence right now. It's also fun not doing anything, right?' — and rather than returning to Phase 5 the rep put one line of pressure on it and presented the price about three minutes later. The script's instruction is explicit that hesitation sends you back to Phase 5, and this is the pivot on which the call was lost.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted — 'Are you ready to get rolling?' — but no agreement was reached, so none of the payment or onboarding steps became reachable.

objection_plays.detail: Most of the play ran in substance across roughly twenty minutes and none of it landed. What ran: the can-it-get-you-there question, asked earlier in P6; 'what do you need to think about?' and 'Outside of the money, like, why do you have a commitment issue?' as the what's-actually-coming-up move; a close variant of thinking-versus-deciding — 'is it about thinking about it, or is it more so about just making an excuse to think about it?'; the pattern callback — 'you've been on and off the whole time, then now it's vacation mode, and after vacation mode, you might get started, and then something happens again'; and the are-you-sure test — 'Are you saying that just to get off the call with me, or are you saying that because you're genuinely thinking about it?'. What did not run: 'What makes you feel it can?' and the identity move, 'That man you want to be — how does HE decide right now?', which was the obvious play given twenty minutes of kids, grandkids and shame material already on the table.

World Cup travel was raised as the reason not to start now. The never-the-right-time move ran strongly — 'there's never going to be the right time to actually do something. Not now, not in five years, not in 10 years, not in a hundred years' — along with 'there's also people actually taking action when there is a World Cup'. Not run: the busy-season question, 'What if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled?', and most notably 'the longer you wait the harder this gets — metabolism slows, injuries compound', which was the single most applicable line in the play for a man with ten years of degenerating back pain.

A textbook fear and doubt trigger and no play ran against it. The prospect stated it plainly — 'my mindset is not fixed to succeed because I've failed so many times' — and then handed over his own burned-before metaphor, the shark that stops hitting the glass after being blocked so many times that it stops trying even when the glass is removed. The play's own burned-before move ('if you got hurt in a relationship once, do you never trust again?') was sitting there pre-built by the prospect and was not used. No certainty question, no bridge, no plane. The rep returned to the excuse frame instead.

Clinical fit. The prospect opened the call with it — 'the only thing is the issue that I have right now is like, how can I protect my back from not injuring myself?' — and returned to it at the close. There is no scripted path, as already logged from the Tyron Giuliani call, and the improvisation was a family anecdote about the rep's father's hernia, a twice-repeated 'we're not doctors' disclaimer, and then a flat reassurance that contradicted the disclaimer: 'that's not gonna happen'. Nobody asked whether a clinician had assessed him.

Prepayment and irreversibility. The objection was not capacity to pay — he ruled that out explicitly — but exposure: $6,000 non-cancellable against a condition that has flared repeatedly for a decade, versus the $200/month subscription he could cancel. Objection C has no answer for this because it assumes the blocker is money. The rep justified the upfront as a commitment device and cited an informal pause precedent for another client, which is the right raw material but was delivered as an anecdote rather than a term.

notes: The best discovery in the batch — Phases 3, 4 and 5 ran close to complete and produced genuinely deep material — attached to the two failures that decided it. He presented price against 'I'm on the fence right now' instead of returning to Phase 5, and when fear surfaced he had no play for it despite the prospect handing him the metaphor to use. The structural lesson for the script: this prospect's two real objections, clinical fit and prepayment exposure, both fall in the gaps, and neither is a rep failure.
